nameStory: Bushgrass gets its name from its tendency to form dense, bush-like clumps that can dominate areas where it establishes. The 'grass' part is obvious, but this species creates such thick, tall stands that early botanists thought it resembled shrubby vegetation more than typical lawn grasses. It's also called wood small-reed, reflecting its preference for woodland edges and its relationship to other reedgrasses.
description: Bushgrass is a tall, clumping perennial grass that forms dense colonies through underground stems called rhizomes. It typically grows 2-5 feet tall with narrow, flat leaves and feathery flower clusters that appear in late summer. This European native has a robust, almost shrub-like appearance when growing in large patches. The grass produces airy, purplish-brown seed heads that catch the light beautifully in late season.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, upright clumps that spread by underground rhizomes, creating thick colonies that feel almost impenetrable when you try to walk through them

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Flat, narrow leaves about 1/4 inch wide with rough edges that feel slightly scratchy when you run your finger along them; leaves are blue-green to gray-green in color

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Loose, feathery flower clusters (panicles) that start purplish and fade to tan or brown; each tiny flower has silky hairs that give the whole seed head a soft, fuzzy appearance

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small seeds with long, white silky hairs attached that help them float on the wind; shake a mature seed head and watch the fluffy seeds drift away like tiny parachutes

habitat: In New England, bushgrass typically grows in disturbed areas, woodland edges, and open fields, particularly in locations with average to moist soil conditions. It can tolerate a range of moisture levels from normal garden soil to wet areas near marshes. You're most likely to encounter it in areas that have been cleared or disturbed, where it can quickly establish dense colonies.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge from established clumps, growing rapidly as temperatures warm. The fresh spring growth has a bright green color that's quite different from the mature plant.
seasonality.summer: Leaves reach full size and the plant focuses on vegetative growth, spreading through underground rhizomes. Flower buds begin forming in late summer.
seasonality.fall: Produces its distinctive feathery flower clusters in late August through September, which mature to fluffy seed heads by October. Seeds disperse on autumn winds.
seasonality.winter: Dried stems and seed heads persist through winter, appearing as tan to golden-brown clumps that rustle in the wind and provide winter interest.

funFact: Despite being called 'small-reed,' bushgrass is actually an incredibly aggressive spreader that can take over entire fields in just a few years - a single plant can produce over 300 new shoots in one growing season through its underground network!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Canadian bluejoint, which also forms tall clumps, but Canadian bluejoint has more open, spreading flower clusters and typically grows in wetter areas. Remember: bushgrass clusters are denser and bushier, while bluejoint is more gracefully arching.
contextualKnowledge: Bushgrass is a non-native species from Europe that's considered invasive in some areas due to its aggressive spreading habit. While it's currently uncommon in New England with only 21 recorded observations, land managers keep an eye on it because of its potential to dominate native plant communities.
compareHints: Compared to its native relatives like Canadian bluejoint and Northern reedgrass, bushgrass forms much denser, more impenetrable colonies and has a more robust, almost shrub-like growth habit. Canadian bluejoint tends to be more graceful and open, while Northern reedgrass is typically smaller and less aggressive. Bushgrass also tolerates drier conditions better than most of its moisture-loving native cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American marram grass differs from its inland relatives like Canadian bluejoint by its exclusively coastal habitat and inward-curling leaves.

Among its reedgrass relatives, Canadian bluejoint is distinguished by its preference for inland wetlands rather than coastal areas (unlike American marram grass) and its loose, feathery flower clusters rather than dense, compact ones.
Northern reedgrass differs from its cousin Canadian bluejoint by being less robust overall and preferring cooler, more northern conditions.
Among its Calamagrostis relatives, Pickering's Reed Bentgrass is more delicate than the robust Canadian Bluejoint and lacks the beach-dwelling habit of American Marram Grass.
Compared to its more common relative Canadian Bluejoint, Slim-stem Small-reedgrass is much smaller overall with notably thinner stems and a more delicate appearance.
